speechtext: Hon. W. D. EULER (Minister of Trade and Commerce) moved that the second and final report of the special committee on the marketing of wheat and other grains, presented on Thursday, June 11, be concurred in.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to say a word before the
TMr. Bennett.]
report presented by the special committee is concurred in, because the producers of western Canada may regard it as very brief. I think it is only fair to say to the public and to hon. members of this house who were not members of the committee that the committee were of the unanimous opinion that nothing should be done to injure or jeopardize the sale of our wheat and that nothing should be done to handicap the board in its selling operations. The evidence was somewhat confusing, but once the majority of the committee had decided that a royal commission should be set up to review the evidence taken and to carry on further investigation, it was felt that no useful purpose could be served by further discussion or by going into more detail with respect to the evidence.
It is true the report is brief. One paragraph in particular might be termed a majority and minority opinion. It states that there was no conclusive evidence that the board had protected1 speculative shorts, and it states also that the committee found no conclusive evidence on that point. I think this brief explanation in due to the public and I do not believe any useful purpose can be served by further reviewing the evidence. With this explanation, I am prepared to concur in the report.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to say a word or two, having been a member of the committee appointed to investigate this particular question. I am glad that we brought in a unanimous report and that a further investigation is to be undertaken to find the best method of marketing our grain. May I take this opportunity to present a resolution passed by one of the farmer organizations in my constituency. It is typical of others that I have received. I received this particular one some months ago and have taken up the matter with the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Euler). The resolution reads:
That whereas there being a guaranteed minimum price established for wheat, and no protection afforded coarse grainB, we are of the opinion that unless there is a radical change in the coarse grain situation before seeding time 1936, there will be a very large increase in the acreage seeded to wheat.
Therefore we the shareholders of this association strongly urge that the principles contained in section 14 of the Canadian Wheat Board Act be applied by which coarse grains may be brought under the operation of the Canadian wheat board.
A. W. Hawker,
Secretary,
Oakville Elevator Association.
If I may be allowed a moment or two, I should like to say a word with regard to the

Wheal and Other Grains
grain situation. The people in the district from ivhich I come and throughout the province of Manitoba realize the danger of overproduction in wheat and have been switching gradually to the growing of barley. The barley crop in western Canada is becoming increasingly important. If we could produce more barley and less wheat, I think all hon. members will agree that it would be in the interests not only of the farmers but of the whole of Canada. We can produce a splendid quality of barley in western Canada; all we require is a market for this grain. There has been considerable investigation with regard to the finding of markets for our barley. During recent years the government of Manitoba has endeavoured to find 'better markets for barley. Doctor Grant was appointed in 1929 to investigate the possibilities in this regard.
The British brewers made a survey of Canada with regard to the quality of barley grown here. They found that our barley was of a superior grade and could be used for malting purposes, but they also found that the best grades were being used by the Canadian and American brewers. They were getting only the poorer grades. They complained that the malting barley they were getting from the terminal elevators in Canada was mixed and unsuitable for malting purposes. They found that the 3 C.W. barley contained many weed seeds and frosted grains and other foreign matter which made it useless as a malting barley. The eastern Canadian farmers have declared that our 3 C.W. barley contains too many weed seeds. They do not want to buy this barley even for the purpose of hog feed. I should like to read an extract from an editorial which appeared in the Manitoba Tribune, as follows:
British maltsters are not the only ones to complain. Speaking to the national barley committee this week in Toronto, Professor R. G. Knox of the Guelph agricultural college, said that if western growers wanted a better eastern market they would have to send out a product free from weed seeds. "The great prevalence of weed seeds in western barley," he said, "was a serious handicap to its sale to Ontario hog raisers as feed.
What we want is another grade of barley, suitable for malting purposes, which will be stored in special bins in the terminal elevators where it will be available to foreign buyers and be guaranteed as suitable for malting purposes.
I should like to place on record a resolution passed by the Portage local of the United Farmers of Manitoba. I shall hurry with this, sir, as I know you do not expect any extended remarks at this time. It reads:
Be it resolved whereas the descriptions and definitions of "statutory grades" of barley are reproduced in accordance with schedule one of the new Canada Grain Act on grades of barley, whereas the act reads "number three extra six row barley shall weigh 48 pounds and equal in value for malting purposes to
O.A.C. '21," we find that many samples of malting varieties going forward for inspection only grade three C.W. on account of being under the weight of 48 pounds and whereas many cars being inspected that weigh 46 pounds to 47 pounds are graded three C.W. barley or lower according to weight, it is resolved at this meeting that a new grade of six row barley be established for malting barley that weighs between 46 and 48 pounds. We suggest a grade of 4 extra six row barley. Due to the fact that the existing spreads between three C.W. barley of malting variety and three extra six row barley of malting variety have been too wide during the past two years, running from 2 to 35 cents per bushel, with only one pound difference in the weight, it is therefore apparent that the malting companies have derived considerable values on malting barley under the weight of 48 pounds.
Respectfully submitted to your government.
It is a well known fact that barley weighing less than 48 pounds to the bushel is being used by Canadian maltsters. Barley weighing 47 pounds is fit for the maltsters and is being used by Canadian maltsters at the present time, but simply because our regulations do not allow barley weighing less than 48 pounds to the bushel to be classed as six-row, we are losing a special market which would be available. This resolution therefore asks the government to give us a new grade between six-row and 3 C.W., weighing less than 48 pounds and guaranteeing a purer quality for the buyers overseas. I suggest that this barley be special binned on reaching the terminal elevators and not mixed with foreign matter as I have indicated in my remarks. I have taken the question up with the Minister of Trade and Commerce and he in turn has taken it up with the head of the grain commission, who has pointed out that the grain act will be completely overhauled next year when this matter will be taken into consideration. There is nothing to prevent the grain board from giving us the benefit of this new grade in order to take care of the 1936 crop, and for that reason I am on my feet, urging the government to see that this is undertaken.

Representing as I do a large grain
producing constituency in western Canada, I wish to concur in the remarks just made by the preceding speakers, the hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Perley) and the hon. member for Portage la Prairie (Mr. Leader),
Questions

but particularly would I impress upon the government the fact that in western Canada there is a desire that the government shall make an unqualified pronouncement in favour of continuing a wheat board, and setting an adequate price for wheat and other grains. That is the issue which is engaging the minds of the producers of western Canada at the present time, and I hope this will be done at no far distant date.

speechtext:
The house resumed, from Tuesday, June 16, consideration of the motion of Hon. Mr. Dunning for the third reading of Bill No. 82, to amend the Bank of Canada Act.
Mr. J. S. WOODSWORTH (Winnipeg North Centre); Yesterday the house spent the entire day in discussing what words should appear on the bank notes, or more properly speaking, what languages should appear on
[Mr. McLean.1
the bank notes. It seems to me there are other aspects of this legislation that are of immensely greater importance to the people of Canada, and which we are in danger of overlooking almost entirely. For some years we in our group have urged a government owned and controlled central bank; indeed we have gone so far as to urge the nationalization of our entire banking system. I admit frankly that unless the monetary policy is changed, government control of the central bank would not bring the desired results. I admit further that under this or any other government dominated by capitalist ideals no fundamental changes are likely. But I would urge that government control is a step at least in the right direction, and again, that a central bank controlled by the government would be necessary in order to carry out the policies which we in the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation advocate.
It is not my purpose to-day to make any extended speech. Our position has been stated on the resolution and in the committee. May I summarize what we have tried to say? We believe that this central bank as constituted cannot perform the functions which a central bank should perform. We believe that this legislation is a surrendering of sovereignty in the monetary field. Whether the parliament of Canada ever had that sovereignty is, perhaps, a matter to be discussed; but in any case we have in the central bank a more powerful instrument than w-e have ever had before, and as we see it, this instrument is being-given over into private hands and Canada cannot be sovereign in that monetary field under the existing arrangement. Again, this legislation grants special1 privileges and powers to a group of shareholders who constituted a very small proportion of the citizens of Canada. Further, this legislation does not, as we see it, implement the promises made by the Liberals during the election. Yesterday some of the Liberal members claimed that they had a mandate with regard to what language should be placed on government bills. I cannot see that they had any mandate with regard to that matter, .because it was not generally discussed at the election, but I think they did have a mandate to carry out certain financial or monetary reforms. Undoubtedly all over the country many Liberals said that if their party were returned to power we shoulcj have a national central bank. I do not want to go over the field again. I want just to put that on record. In my judgment the general belief was that if the Liberals were returned

Bank nj Canada-Mr. Woodsworth
to power we would have a nationally owned and controlled central bank. I do not believe this legislation gives us that.
So far there has not been an opportunity formally to place our position on record or to ascertain what support it has in this house. I attempted during the resolution stage to move an amendment, but it was ruled out of order. Possibly I could have moved on the second reading a resolution similar to that which I propose to move to-day. As a matter of fact the Speaker passed so quickly over the second reading that, although I was in the house and paying attention to the proceedings, I had not the opportunity to move my resolution. So I take this occasion to place our position on record.
As it has become almost the practice since the Liberals have been in power with such a large majority to challenge, as being out of order practically any motion that is made-

I could have moved to refer this bill back to the committee of the whole, as we so frequently do, for further consideration or with instructions that the committee have power to do certain things, but I knew perfectly well that if we offered any fundamental changes in a bill affecting finance we would be confronted immediately with the old objection that no private member may move to alter the financial structure of a bill.

speechtext:
I know it paid
more but I am speaking of the par value, and further I am speaking regarding a point of order. The minister did not rely upon that particular point of order but found refuge in another, that since this bill in its original form had been approved by the governor general we could not make any alterations in it. Well, that seems to me to be carrying the powers of the governor general to an altogether unwarranted degree. However, it was on such grounds that my amendment was ruled out of order. I suggest now that, thanks to the wisdom of our ancestors or our predecessors in parliament, we may still express our opinions, unless indeed accepted rules are to be entirely disregarded.
We believe that this bill is designed to somewhat improve the situation; it looks in the direction of greater government control, and for that reason we propose to vote for the bill. I should like that to be understood. On the other hand we do not believe the bill goes far enough. I should like to point out that my amendment, if carried, will not kill the bill. There are always some timorous souls in the house who are afraid of what might happen if tlhe bill were to be killed. I do not think there is any danger that the amendment will pass while the government have such a large majority, but these members think they should vote as though the amendment might carry and they fear that then the bill might be killed. Let me reassure them. If the amendment carries the bill is not killed: its passage is simply delayed. On that point I should

like to direct attention to a rule appearing in May at page 392. May is here speaking of the second reading of a bill, though as I have said our authorities, both Beauchesne and Bourinot, state that what is true of the second reading is also true of the third reading. May says:
It must be borne in mind, however, that the resolution, if agreed to, does not arrest the progress of the bill, the second reading of which may be moved on another occasion.
The effect of such an amendment is merely to supersede the question for now reading the bill a second time;-
Let me note that the "now" is in italics.
And the bill is left in the same position as if the question for now reading the bill a second time had been simply negatived or superseded by the previous question. The house refuses, on that particular day, to read the bill a second time, and gives its reasons for such refusal: but the bill is not otherwise disposed of. Such being the technical effect of a resolution, so carried, it need scarcely be said that its moral and political results vary according to the character and importance of the resolution itself, the support it has received, and the means there may be of meeting it, in the further progress of the bill.

Let me proceed a step further. I have said it was on February 27, 1933, that the Liberal party made the pronouncement it did in this House of Commons with respect to the creation of a properly constituted national central bank, as one of a series of policies it intended to fight for to the end of that parliament and to carry, if necessary, from parliament to the people. It continued to advocate these policies in this house, but it was not until July 31, 1933, that the government of the day accepted the view of the Liberal party that something in the nature of a national central bank was necessary. I should perhaps not say that they accepted it at that time, but rather that they accepted the view that it was necessary to inquire into the matter and to that end appointed a royal commission on banking and currency in Canada. The commission recommended the creation of a central national bank.
I hope I made clear the fact that it was the Liberal party which put forward in 1932, as a part of its program, the establishment of a properly constituted national central bank; that it was the Liberal party which advocated that policy in this House of Commons to the point that it became necessary for the then government .to recognize the necessity of having the matter inquired into, which advocacy brought about the appointment of a royal commission; that the commission endorsed the view of the Liberal party of Canada, previously and continuously expressed, that there should be a national central bank. In the following year, 1934, as a consequence, there was introduced a bill for the creation of a national central bank.
The attitude of the Liberal party with respect to the functions the bank should discharge was set forth very clearly in the course of the discussion on that bill. Our position was stated in the course of debate time and again by myself as leader of the party. Hon. gentlemen know that within the ranks of a great political party, while there may be one general view on which all are united, there are shades of opinion which tend towards one extreme or the other. That is true of every great gathering of human beings, but the Liberal party in its pronouncements, in the terms I have read to the house, stood for the thing upon which it was possible for all to agree. In the course of debate it became necessary to expand our views a little, in particular with regard to the question of whether there should be any private directors on the board at all and with regard to the question of whether government ownership was an absolute essential for a properly

constituted national central bank. I contend that there; is no possible room for doubt as to the position then taken by the opposition having regard to what was said by myself in this house as leader of the party. I refer first to what was said on .the second reading of the bill. This will be found in Hansard of March 8, 1935, where again I set forth the functions of a central bank as we had contended all along they should be:
A central bank, as we view it, differs from other banks in that its function is primarily regulatory and controlling-and not commercial in the sense of being intended primarily for private profit or gain. In other words, the function of a central bank in the world of banking and finance, as we view it, is that of subordinating the special to the general interest or. to express the matter more concretely, that of subordinating the private interest in banking and credit to the public interest. In no sense should the bank be, or be permitted to become, a banker's bank. It is and ought to be a government bank, the government being representative of the interests of the country as a whole. Its main purpose is and should be to protect the public interest in banking and credit.
That was on the second reading of the measure. The other day my hon. friend the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) gave other quotations from some of the statements I made during the course of the discussion in this house. One of those quotations will be found in Hansard of June 1, 1936, as taken from page 4228 of the revised Hansard of 1934. This statement sets forth very clearly what was in the mind1 of the.Liberal party. Addressing my right hon. friend, who was then Prime Minister, I said:
The Prime Minister will notice that at the moment I am not suggesting the government should own the bank. I am not at the moment discussing the question of ownership at all. As I said last night. I think the question of ownership is debatable.
I said that at the beginning of the discussions; I said throughout the discussions and during the campaign, and I repeat it now: I think the question of ownership is debatable, for reasons which appear in what I have said repeatedly in this house. I do not think the question of effective control is debatable. I think if you have effective public control it matters relatively little where the ownership rests, but if you have not effective public control then ownership in full may be desirable should it prove to be the only way to acquire it. At the time, speaking of the importance of effective public control, I went on to say:
I am however discussing the question of control of policy, and I do say that with respect to policies, whether they relate to trade, to shipping, to marketing, to finance, to defence, or to any other phase of a country's economy, those policies, if they are the expression of view of a government representative

Bank of Canada-Mr. Mackenzie King
of the people, should be capable of being carried out without interference from any institution whatever, but rather with the sympathetic cooperation of all institutions. That is the only way in which in a country we can have either democratic or responsible government.
During the course of his speech in this house on June 1 the Minister of Finance made further reference to my remarks on- June 22, 1934, when I gave my reasons for believing that there might be wisdom in having on a board of directors, even as representative of private interests, some men with special knowledge of the great commercial1 and financial interests of the country. Let me say this: For the life of me I cannot see why it should be assumed always that private interests and public interests are necessarily opposed to each other I believe that in the long run it will be found that the thing wLich is most in the public interest ultimately will prove to be best for private interests. Take any of these great public utilities, street railways or the like; let them operate in any way other than that which tends best to serve the public interest and in their private interests they begin to suffer immediately. However there may be and undoubtedly there are times, and I have made that clear in what I have quoted from my speech at Seaforth, when private institutions may view matters exclusively from the point of view of the interests of their immediate shareholders and investors, and that the private interest may be contrary to the public interest. When such times come, and there is a conflict between private and public interest then at all such times the public interest should be made to prevail.
But there may also be times when those exercising or seeking to exercise control in the public interest may be mistaken in their views or the course they may wish to pursue. They may err in judgment, and if they do they make serious and grievous mistakes with regard to matters which affect the credit of the country as a whole and the interests private as well as public of all its citizens. I would ask the representatives of the people in this House of Commons whether on such occasions it is not in the public interest to have, if he can be found, some individual, associated if you like with private interests, who will be in a position to direct the attention of his colleagues, and through his colleagues or in other ways direct the attention of government and of parliament and of the public to what is an apparently mistaken course of procedure before it is taken and it is too late to remedy it? I say that in great transactions which affect the well-being of the industrial and financial and commercial life of the
country, too much in the way of special knowledge cannot be obtained. I have sufficient faith in the power of truth of itself to believe that no man, whether representing private or public interests, can get anywhere with representations which he may make unless those representations have a substantial element of truth behind them. I said to my right hon. friend at the time we were discussing the matter of direction, because I thought he was one who had had experience with large business in a large way, that I thought he ought to be the first to appreciate the necessity of having check and countercheck in all matters of this kind. The situation was reversed at the time. I was pointing out the need of directors appointed to represent the public interest in addition to directors selected by private interests. I did so in the following words:
I think my right hon. friend must agree that in these matters of large finance, cheek and counter check is wholly advisable. It is advisable in financial transactions of a limited size, and it is more necessary as well as advisable in those of considerable size. But here are financial transactions of the greatest magnitude conceivable, and check and counter check are imperative. I do think the directorate of the bank ought to be so formed that, whether the pressure is upon the bank from the government on the one side, or upon the government from the financial interests and through the bank on the other, there should be on the board of directors some one or more persons who will be quick to sense the situation, give the danger signal, and arouse the country to the pressure which is being brought to bear. There is the danger of a government bringing too much in the way of pressure to hear on a central bank. On the other hand, there is equal danger of the financial interests that are allied with the banks bringing influence to bear upon a government. There will be both these dangers always, and the only way in Which that possibility can be lessened is by making sure that both powers, the money power and the power of government, are represented on a common board so that one or the other will be in a position to direct the attention of the people at large to the dangers which they may see developing in the affairs of an institution which is or ought to be a great national trust.
In the face of a statement of that kind, made in this parliament and recorded in Hansard, a volume which all hon. members of parliament know well, and which statement was there all through the general election campaign, how can anyone say that as leader of the Liberal party I stood for complete government ownership of the national bank? I made it repeatedly clear that I thought the question of ownership was debatable, but I went much further and pointed out wherein there would be a distinct advantage in having private interests as well as government interests represented on a board of a properly consti-

tuted national central bank, so long as care was taken to see that the effective control rested with the government through its nominees on the directorate and in other ways.
That is not the only statement which I made on this phase of the matter. On the third reading of the bill, when my right hon. friend had spoken and stated that we had said some things over and over again, I said I thought they needed to be said once more, as apparently up to that time they had not made any real impression on him. I then made quite clear my own position. Here are the words I used, as they appear in Hansard of 1934, at page 4361:
Speaking for myself, may I repeat that I can see wherein the question of public ownership of a state bank may well be a debatable question. I regard it as debatable for the reason that there is much to be said on both sides.
Then I gave the reasons. Here is one objection to complete public ownership of a central bank which I pointed out. I ask if it is not pertinent to much that is being said on monetary matters in our own country at this very time:
The objections that I see, so far as it can be named an objection, to public ownership of a central bank is that it may raise in the minds of the people of the country many expectations which may not be capable of ever being realized. Many will believe that because the state owns the central bank it will be able to meet each and every disorder that may arise in the country from any financial cause. We here all know that a state-owned institution any more than a privately-owned institution, will not be able to do anything of the kind. At the same time there would be occasioned the thought in the minds of many people that having set up a publicly-owned institution we had discovered a public remedy for all social and financial ills. I do not think it is advisable, or in the public interest at any time, for parliament to create in the minds of the people at large expectations which are not capable of being realized.
In the second place, I believe there is always a possible danger to the position of the state itself in the event of anything untoward happening to a bank which is owned by the state. There may quickly arise in the public mind confusion between what may be matter confined in its effects to the bank, and what may be assumed to concern the very life of the state itself. This may not happen so much within the bounds of the country where the situation may be known and understood as beyond its confines, and in the minds of peoples of other nations.
And I gave examples of how panics have arisen in the state because of the identification in the public mind of some government-owned institution with the state itself. I was most careful to point all this out, because I believed and do believe very firmly, that a government cannot be too careful, that any

political party cannot be too careful, about raising in the public mind expectations which cannot be satisfied, or in any way claiming for an institution which has to do with the issue of money and currency, powers which it is well known in the last resort cannot be exercised in ways which some may be led to' believe they can.
In the same speech I added:
I wish at this time to make clear the grounds upon which I personally have advocated the institution! of a central bank and the grounds upon which the Liberal party has made the institution of a public bank part of its policy.
I then restated what I have read here from the statement of government policy as given in 1933, and when I came to certain words I emphasized them:
... to perform the functions of rediscount, and the control of currency issue, considered in terms of public need.
Following those words "in terms of public need," I said:
Note "in terms of public need" not possible private gain.
I was making very clear the contrast intended, making very clear at every stage in the discussion that there were certain distinct limitations upon a central bank, and that to create any false impression with regard to what the government, through an agency of this kind, could or might do was only working an injury to the people of the country.
May I conclude with this last reference,
I wish to include it, because here I stated the issue between the then government and the Liberal party very clearly, and I stated it in terms of an issue. At page 4363 of Hansard of 1934 I am reported as follows:
That is the issue, as I see it, the crux of the whole situation-whether this parliament, representing the people of Canada, is to create a great financial institution which is to control the credit and currency of the country, place that institution in private hands, both as to ownership and control, hand over to this privately-owned and controlled institution many of the functions and powers which the government itself at the present time is exercising, part in large measure with w-hat the government now possess in the way of control of credit, part with what it possesses at the present time in the matter of the right of issuing currency, and hand over gold reserves and securities which are at the present moment in its possession-all this to be handed over to an institution which is to be privately-owned and controlled, or whether the institution to which these rights, powers, possessions and privileges are to be given is to be subject to an effective measure of government control.
That, I think is a very serious situation, and there is no argument, it seems to me, which it is possible to bring forward that can really

Bank of Canada-Mr. Mackenzie King
defend action of that kind on the part of this parliament. If it were of necessity a choice solely between the extreme of absolute government ownership and government control on the one hand, and on the other complete private ownership and private control, I could understand that there might be many who would find it difficult to decide one way or the other, there being no possibility of a middle course which would help to avoid what would be regarded as the dangers in either extreme. But there is a middle course, and it is that middle cimrse which the government is apparently unwilling even to consider at the present time. That middle course would be to enable the government-
And I ask hon. members to see whether this legislation does not implement to the full what was there stated as the Liberal party's position:

to appoint a certain number of directors, a number sufficient to give the government control of the central bank, directors who would not own shares but would represent the government, and who would sit along with the directors who were the nominees of those who owned the shares. Short of complete government ownership and control, could there be anything in the interests of all classes generally which obviously would serve the common interest better than that? One group of directors would be watching the actions of the bank from the point of view of investors, and the other group would be watching the actions of the bank from the point of view of the interests of the public at large; and these two in conference from day to day would undoubtedly be able to prevent many extreme actions being taken which might be contrary to the public interest, and they would also be able to bring about that unity and continuity, in the affairs of the bank which the Prime Minister regards as so all-important.
Those statements do not permit of any doubt as to their meaning. They are as clear-cut and frank as statements can possibly be. May I read this one further statement as presenting the major objection of the Liberal party to the Bank of Canada as it was being constituted by the then government?
The present legislation, establishing the Bank of Canada, is a definite step in the establishment of an imperial policy of finance, under which the financial destiny of Canada is placed under persons independent of parliament, who can maintain, through the Bank of England and the other central banks of empire nations, a definite and positive control of empire currency, credit and trade. That being the case, I feel very strongly that this measure ought to be reconsidered before we are asked to vote upon it.
The Bank of Canada, as constituted by this proposed enactment, will undoubtedly be the means of vesting in the Bank of England the management and control of Canada's foreign exchange and Canada's internal credit administration. As I said the other evening, once a nation parts with the control of its currency and credit, it matters not who makes the nation's laws. Usury, once in control, will wreck any nation. Until the control of the issue of currency and credit is restored to government and recognized as its most conspicuous and sacred responsibility, all talk of
the sovereignty of parliament and of democracy is idle and futile. Those are strong words; they constitute a strong argument, and they are words of which this house ought to take full account before it is too late.
I say, Mr. Speaker, that paragraph makes perfectly clear what I meant when I spoke about the control of currency issue and credit being the most conspicuous and sacred responsibility of government. I was speaking there of whether the great financial powers were to control in policies relating to finance, or whether the government of the day, responsible to the will of the people, was to control in the matter of giving effect to these policies. I said that as the act was then framed all control by parliament through its representatives was being wholly removed, and that what was necessary was to bring back that control and to see that it would be effectively exercised in the interests of the people.
I touched amongst other things upon the struggle that Mr. Gladstone had with the Bank of England, and showed how Mr. Gladstone himself had found the bank, instead of being a help to the government, was often an obstacle, and that he had to overcome difficulties with the bank before he could get his own government policies under way. I pointed out that what was necessary was that no institution, and least of all a great banking institution, should ever be created in this country with any such power, or be so constituted that it could be a force to oppose the will of the government of the day. I said that what was necessary was to get the central bank into a position where the government of the day would be in a position to control its policy. Speaking of my right hon. friend's measure as it was then I said:
That is exactly what the government proposes to see is done by this bill in its present form. In matters of finance it makes the bank supreme; it makes the bank the body that will determine the monetary policy of the country, that will have the power to enforce that policy and to resist any monetary policy that may run counter to it. This privately owned and privately controlled institution is to be permitted to do that. The government itself is not to be a substantive power.
It was that point of view which I presented so strongly to the electorate in the campaign when I asserted that if the Liberal party were returned to power the first thing we would seek to do would be to restore to the control of the government the powers which had existed under the Finance Act, and which had been taken away from the government and had been given to this privately owned and privately controlled institution. I said we would restore these powers to the government so that it could effectively control the
3812	COMMONS
Bank oj Canada-Mr. Mackenzie King
bank, and that we would constitute the bank accordingly.
There have been a good many quotations from speeches made in the campaign. I have already referred to what was said in this House of Commons, and which being on the records of this house was available to all speakers in the campaign, if they wished to refer to the exact words of the leader of the Liberal party in setting out what the policy of the party was. There have been many references to press clippings and the like, but I notice that one reference has been significantly omitted, and it is the most important of all. The omission is also most significant.
In stating the policies of a government or a political party there is no way in which those policies can be more effectively and unmistakably stated than over the radio. It is not possible for a leader of a political party to make an address over the radio and have his address subsequently printed and distributed and then say that he did not make the pronouncement which was then made. I ask why it is that throughout the whole of this debate, in referring to what was the policy of the Liberal party as stated by the Liberal leader in the campaign, not a single member has quoted what was said by myself in presenting to the electorate over the radio the policy of the party in respect to currency and credit.
I have in my hand a copy of the addresses I delivered over the radio during the eom-paign, and I refer now to one which I claim is authoritative and authoritative above all others. It is the second radio address I delivered; it was delivered on August 2, 1935. It was an address of Liberal principles and policies, a statement of the Liberal party's position on present day problems. These are the words I used in setting forth the Liberal party's policy in the matter of the control of credit, and I ask again hon. gentlemen to say if in all particulars the pledge which was made over the radio is not being faithfully carried out to the letter in the legislation which is now before us. I said:
The Liberal party-
I began by repeating over the radio the statement which I had made in this House of Commons in 1933, and which at different times and in different places I continued to make throughout the country.
The Liberal party believes that credit is a ublic matter, not of interest to bankers only, ut of direct concern to the average citizen.
It stands for the immediate establishment of a properly constituted national central bank, to perform the functions of rediscount, and the control of currency issue* considered in terms of public need. A central bank is necessary to determine the supply of currency in relation 
to the domestic, social and industrial requirements of the Canadian people; and also to deal with problems of international commerce and exchange.
As a national central bank has been established by the present government since this statement of Liberal policy was issued, I feel it necessary to say here that the Bank of Canada as established is far from being the institution contemplated by the Liberal party. The Bank of Canada is, as more than one of our leading economists has said, of the fascist type. It is a private corporation, with power to control the volume of the country's credit. Let me repeat what I said in parliament in protesting against the surrender to a private institution of the state's control over the nation's currency and credit:
"Once a nation parts with the control of its currency and credit, it matters not who makes the nation's laws. Usury, once in control, will wreck any nation. Until the control of the issue of currency and credit is restored to government and recognized as its most conspicuous and sacred responsibility, all talk of the sovereignty of parliament and of democracy is idle and futile."
To regain for the nation what has been lost and to secure a properly constituted national central bank, will continue to be a first objective of Liberal effort.
There is the pledge which was given to the people of 'Canada over the radio by myself as the leader of the party. I say that every word and every line of that pledge is being literally and absolutely fulfilled in the legislation that is before us.
Let me now go one step further. Reference has been made to what I said to the public on the night of the great Liberal victory of the significance of the results. The statement which was subsequently issued in the form of a leaflet entitled the Voice of the People, was made on October 14, 1935. Here is what I said in reference to the central bank and the control of credit:
The election is an endorsation of the Libera] view that credit is a public matter, not of interest to bankers only, but of direct concern to every citizen. It is a verdict against a privately owned and controlled central bank, and in favour of a properly constituted national bank to perform the functions of rediscount, and the control of currency issue considered in terms of public need. There can be no mistaking the demand for a restoration to the government of Canada of control over credit and currency issue. As the campaign proceeded, the issue of the control, by the people, of all functions of government, through their representatives in parliament, and not by any other power, became increasingly clear. The electorate has declared that a responsible ministry, not organized finance and international money power, is to control in all matters of state.
I ask if that statement in what it foreshadowed was not on all fours with the statements made during the days of the election, and whether that statement is not being literally and absolutely fulfilled in the legislation which is before us at the moment?

Bank of Canada-Mr. Mackenzie King

How can the
Prime Minister say that the present bill contemplates control by the bank over credit?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: MAJORITY CONTROL BY GOVERNMENT OF CAPITAL STOCK AND BOARD OF DIRECTORS
speechtext:
That is the main function of the bank, to control the issuance of currency and credit. Referring the other day to this statement by myself, my hon. friend from Winnipeg North Centre said that it was an undertaking to have the government control credit and. currency issue. He did not read the sentence as if the word "restoration," or the words "a restoration to the government," had any significance. He took care not to place any emphasis upon those words. I had pointed out in previous addresses that under the Finance Act, the government of this country, through the Department of Finance, was controlling the issue of currency and credit, it was issuing currency and controlling credit, but that those functions had been taken away from the Department of Finance and given to this privately owned and privately controlled institution. I stated that until this control of credit and the issue of currency were restored to government-which is what we are doing now by this bill-and recognized as its most conspicuous and sacred responsibility, all balk of the sovereignty of parliament and of democracy was idle and futile. I was stressing the importance of these functions being restored to government and discharged by the bank under public control as contrasted with being exercised by a privately owned and controlled institution. Why did I speak of the control of the issue of currency and credit as the most conspicuous and sacred responsibility? It is most conspicuous because without currency and credit there can, be no trade or commerce in the land, and a country organized as a modern country is organized could not carry on its everyday business. It is a sacred responsibility because, unless great care and caution is taken with the way in which currency is issued and credit is controlled, a nation may be quickly brought to disaster.
Something was told the house the other day by the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Cahan) of what he had witnessed in his visits to Germany and other countries of the effect of inflated currencies, not only upon those who had substantial incomes but upon the humblest in the land, upon the mechanics, the artisans, the peasant proprietors and all1 classes and upon their means of livelihood and standards of living. Where there is the power to issue currency and control credit, there is placed the power to bring a nation to disaster unless this power is carefully exercised as a sacred power. That word
"sacred" is the only word that could be appropriately applied to it.
I think I have made very clear and brought up to date the position of the Liberal party as stated by myself as its leader. I challenge any hon. member of this house to find in any place any statement of mine which can be regarded as authoritative, which is at variance, in the slightest particular, with what I have read to this house this afternoon. It cannot be found as it does not exist. The hon. member for York South (Mr. Lawson), acting as the financial critic of the opposition, undertook one afternoon not long ago to criticize this measure. In so doing he characterized it as a delusion and-I cannot at the moment think of the other word he used.

May I read what my hon. friend said at the time. He said:
I say to you, sir, and through you to the members of this committee and the people of this country, that having regard to the statements made by the present Prime Minister throughout the country during the election campaign when he asked the people for votes based on those statements, this measure is a subterfuge and a delusion, and out of the mouth of the present Prime Minister I shall attempt to prove that it is a breach of the pledge he gave to the people.
He then proceeded to quote from clippings from different papers. The hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George said a day or two ago to one of the members of another group that it was inadvisable to proceed in the course of a debate with a scrap album of petty extracts from newspapers, but his own colleague, sitting only two seats from him, had his scrap-book beside him full of petty extracts from newspapers. He sought to make good use of them. I am going to read the extracts which my hon. friend cited, in order that the house may see whether what he quoted, in an effort to show that I was not thoroughly consistent with the position I had taken in this house and elsewhere all through the campaign, was at all at variance with

what I have said and quoted this afternoon. What the hon. member for York South produced at the time represented the search of his entire party through the papers of the country to see what extracts might be discovered to use against the Liberal party at this time. Those extracts, it may be assumed, were the most vulnerable of any that could be found. He said:
First, I should like to refer to a report appearing in Ottawa Citizen of August 3, 1935, reporting a speech made by the present Prime Minister. I quote now what appeared in that newspaper in quotation marks, as being the words of the right hon. gentleman:
"The Liberal party stands for the immediate establishment of a properly constituted national central bank to perform the function of rediscounts and the control of currency issue considered in terms of public need."
Is that not exactly what I have just stated? Some hon. members then said, "hear, hear," and the hon. member for York South continued :
Keep right on. I will soon get to a point where you will not shout "hear, hear."
"Usury, once in control, will wreck any nation. Until the control of the issue of currency and credit is restored to government and recognized as its most conspicuous and sacred responsibility, all talk of sovereignty of parliament and of democracy is idle and futile. To regain for the nation what has thus been lost will continue to be the first objective of Liberal effort."
That was followed by more "hear, hears." Is there anything contradictory there to what was said? Those are the exact words that were used in this house and in the previous statements. The hon. member then continued :
Again I quote from the Ottawa Citizen, this time of August 8, 1935-Mr. Mackenzie King speaking at Kingston; and again I give the words which the newspaper puts in quotation marks:
"He (Mr. Bennett) had taken the gold reserves from the federal treasury, the backing for the country's currency, and' turned them over to a private corporation."
And as the right hon. gentleman travelled west he waxed even more eloquent in that regard, because I observe that according to a report appearing in the Vancouver Sun of September 30, 1935, he had this to say.
He was trying to leave the impression that because I was in Vancouver, where I knew that some of those who had taken an interest in monetary matters held extreme views, I was seeking, if you wish to put it that way, to cater to such extreme views. And what does he quote?
Criticizing Mr. Bennett's bank, he said it was owned and controlled by private stockholders. It had been given by the government $60,000,000 gold reserve and the vast number of securities held by the government from the 
private banks. These were the property of the people of Canada. To-day they belong to the private shareholders of the Bank of Canada, he said.
That is the quotation. Well, is it not true? The statement is there; is there any exception to be taken to it? But let us go further. The hon. gentleman said:
I turn to a report of a speech of the right hon. gentleman contained in the Vancouver Sun of September 30, 1935. I imagine most hon. members of this committee are familiar with the fact that the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation was pretty well in its stride in Vancouver, and is reported so to be in British Columbia.
As I say, seeking to create the impression that there were some who had extreme views to which I was catering. And what does he quote? He goes on:
Out there the right hon. gentleman had this to say:
"We believe that credit should be a social service to serve the needs of the people." "Credit is not the concern of the bankers only but is of concern to you and me."
Credit is to-day controlled by the great international money power. The first step, then, is to establish a national central bank -not another private bank as has been done -but a government bank able to control credit according to the will of the government in matters of great national concern.
The Liberal party believes it is a public matter of direct concern to the average citizen to have a national bank to control currency and credit so that they may serve the public needs.
The first objective is to get back the control that was taken from us. The next is to see that the bank is made national in the truest sense of the word.	[DOT]
That was what I said, speaking to the Canadian Cooperative Commonwealth Federation in Vancouver. Is there one line there that contradicts the statement of policy given officially in this house and the statements of the party, with respect to that policy, as I have read them? Then he goes on, always by insinuation, seeking to leave the impression that something different was said in another place. He comes next to Calgary, where he finds most in evidence not the Canadian Cooperative Commonwealth Federation but the members of the Social Credit party. He directs attention to the fact that Calgary was the centre of social credit, and then he says:
Then the right hon. gentleman went to Alberta where the social credit group appears to have been in its stride. According to a report in the Calgary Daily Herald of October 1, 1935, the right hon. gentleman said.
Now listen to what I said there:
A central bank is necessary to determine the supply of currency in relation to domestic, social and industrial requirements of the Canadian people, and also to deal with problems of international commerce and exchange.

So far the leader of the social credit group might have been making the speech. The right hon. gentleman continued:
"That was a clear statement"-

requirements, and the like, than from the point of view of the interests of capital investors and private bankers only."
Is not the objective as clear and plain as it can be in that statement? The difference is clearly indicated between a bank serving the interests of private investors and a bank which will serve public interests in the sense in which I have described them. I quote further from the hon. gentleman's remarks:
Then he went on.
"Then the government policy, if it were one of extension of credit, would be in a position to put that policy into effect"-
That must be a misprint, because I doubt whether the right hon. gentleman would have repeated the word "policy." I continue:

"through having a central bank which would give more in the way of credit at the time when the need for more in the way of credit was uppermost. And then this last touch, which I think is sublime.
Listen to the sublimity of it:
"We have in the federal field the great issue of monetary reform. I have merely indicated what I have thought was the first step, and if that first is not won then all our efforts at further financial reform so far as the federal field is concerned will be materially impaired."
Will anyone dispute that? Then he quotes further:
"Equality"-
Says the right hon. gentleman to the electors of Alberta.	_	_
-"if they are materially impaired it will have a very serious effect as far as I see it upon the efforts of any province to improve financial conditions there, so I hope when Monday fortnight comes you will think not only what is important to you locally and in a provincial way, but that you will think even more deeply of what is going to be of vital concern to our country with respect to our policy during the next five years."
That was a statement made in the province where social credit was being discussed on all sides. I ask hon. members from that province: Is there a word I said there which is different from what was said in this House of Commons by myself before the election
took place? Then the hon. member for York South concluded with a reference to one other speech which he says was reported in the Vancouver Province of September 21. From that source he quoted me as follows:
Canada is faced with a great battle between the money power and the power of the people -a battle which will be waged in the next parliament. He pleaded for a sweeping Liberal majority in order to carry out his policy of public control of currency and credit, nationalization of the Bank of Canada and monetary reform.
With the word "parliament" the direct quotation ends.
Now this is the only place I have been able to find, in any report anywhere, where mention is made of the words "nationalization of the Bank of Canada." Those words appearing in the report were not mine; they are the reporter's own representation. doubt my hon. friend's search was very diligent. He said that he was proving, out of what he had discovered, that this present measure was a subterfuge and a delusion in the light of statements I had made. Bank oj Canada-Mr. Mackenzie King
the house is a full implementation of what was said by myself as leader of the Liberal party of the party's policy.
I leave this matter now. I hope that the house will vote on the third reading of the measure, so that its records may show how members view a measure which seeks to restore to the government of Canada control of currency issue and of credit, taking back this control from a privately owned and] privately controlled institution and placing it in the hands of a government institution of which the preponderating interest of ownership will be with the government, and over which the government will have effective control. Observe the extent to which that control goes. It is the control, not only of ownership in the preponderating interest, but of an effective directorate, and is the control of the government itself, which has the right to refuse to accept the veto of the governor of the bank where a difference arises with respect to any action of .the directors. Speaking of effective control may I point out that, behind all which takes place by virtue of any power which the government itself may exercise and which the bank itself may attempt to exercise, there must be present at all times to the minds of all concerned the view this parliament is likely to take of whatever transaction is being reviewed. When this act gives to the governor in council power to review any action of the board, where there is a difference between the directors and the governor, and the governor's veto has been exercised, it means that the minute that difference is being discussed, those parties themselves must feel that the difference in question is so important and acute that it is advisable to bring the matter to the attention of the parliament of Canada in order to avoid some great mistake being made. I ask my friends, no matter to which party they belong, is not that in your interests and in mine? We here establish a government controlled central national bank. To-day it is in the control of a Liberal administration. If the Liberal administration, through pressure on the part of its followers or for any other of the alleged reasons that have been given, were capable of having its directors seek to exercise some power in the bank which is not wholly in the public interest, is it not in the interests of all other parties in this country to see that such a move, if at all possible, before it succeeds, is brought up for discussion here on the floor of parliament? When this act takes effect the bank will be under the control of the Liberal administration. It may be under the control of a Conservative administration at some later date.

speechtext:
About four years hence? Then, I say, beware of what may take place four years hence, because then again you will have an effort made to have this bank restored to private ownership and private control. And if an effort is made to have public interests subordinated to private interests, is it not well that there should be an opportunity for this House of Commons and this parliament to know what is the difference of view between those directors who cannot see eye to eye with each other or with the governor, before some far-reaching mistake is made? Similarly I say to my hon. friends of the more radical groups-if I may use that term in its best sense-."Some day you hope to have control of this bank. This bank would then have on it your directors and others. Do you wish to have a bank in which there is to be no opportunity whatever of any possible difference of opinion with respect to the issue of credit and currency being made the subject of debate in this parliament and matters decided by a governor and directors other than your own before you have an opportunity of coming to parliament with power to legislate in a manner which will cause the bank to operate more in accordance with your views?" When we are legislating here we have to think not only of the government which may be in office at the moment but of all the changes that may come with time, changes which may come much more rapidly in times like the present than they have done at any preceding period in the history of the country.
I conclude with this one word. No men who have to do with the responsibilities of government, no men who have to do with what affects the lives and well being of the great masses of the people of this country can wish other than that, if any mistake is being made in connection with financial policy there shall be an opportunity to have the matter discussed on the floor of this house before that mistake takes effect. When hon. gentlemen opposite say it is not in the public interest to have, on a bank which is preponderantly publicly owned, and effectively publicly controlled, a few individuals with special knowledge-knowledge acquired, if you wish, from long business experience with private interests-who may differ if need be with colleagues whom they believe are about to take a wrong course, they belie, in my opinion, the very position that as an opposition they exercise in this house. I am one of those who believe that a government is all the better for having an opposition. The country is all the better for having a government

Bank of Canada-Mr. Cold well
and an opposition, for the reason that men who are absorbed in many great activities may not see all sides of a problem at the same time. Men do not see every angle and aspect of a question when they have a thousand and one different matters to discuss; and when they are determining policy, what is the consideration that, more than anything else, controls a ministry? First of all, their own sense of integrity and right; but secondly, what may be said on the floor of the House of Commons by their political opponents and how the country may view what is so said. In the last resort it is public opinion which controls, and it is in order to inform public opinion and to make public opinion effective as well as to establish an effective government control which will govern this bank in all its actions, that we have adopted the course we have in this legislation.

May I add that, in introducing the remarks he made this afternoon, the Prime Minister did, perhaps unconsciously, an injustice to some of the men who have sat in this chamber. He said that prior to 1932 there was very little in the way of discussion about the central bank. .Yet every year from 1921, when the first Labour member and the first little group of Progressives sat in this house, they brought before parliament again and again the question of a central bank of issue and rediscount, and as the days went on proceeded to develop that policy until it became one of complete nationalization. Those are matters of public record.
I am not going to refer to the speeches of the right hon. gentleman which have been quoted again and again in this house, nor shall I refer to the speeches of various members of the cabinet. In the present debate the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard (Mr. McGeer) has, I think, well expressed the opinion held by hundreds and thousands of people throughout this country, many thousands of whom voted for the Liberal party last October, namely that it was the intention that a Liberal government, when returned to power, would institute a central bank which would ensure to the people of Canada national ownership and national control of both currency and credit.
In the latter portion of the remarks of the right hon. Prime Minister there was one observation that I was surprised to hear. He spoke of the present control of the Bank of Canada as a control of that bank by the Liberal government, and warned the people that subsequently it might be controlled by a Conservative government or by a Cooperative Commonwealth Federation government or some other sort of more radical government which might come in future. That is not my conception of either a nationalized bank or a bank that stands midway between private and national ownership. My conception is this: The government of the day ought to lay down, by and with the advice of parliament, the policies that shall be followed



Bank oj Canada-Mr. Caldwell
in relation to finance, money, currency and credit in this dominion. Then those men engaged or appointed by government should, to the best of their knowledge and ability, carry out those policies in the interests of the people of Canada, and they should do so whether there is in power a Liberal government, a Conservative government or a more radical government. Therefore I was surprised to hear that remark, which may have been made by the right hon. gentleman without intending it to be capable of the interpretation I placed upon it.
Now I should like to say that in my opinion this bill falls far short of what is really required. I have said that a national bank should carry out the policy communicated to it by the government of the day by and with the advice of parliament. Under the present act that is not the case. The Bank of Canada Act is restrictive in most of its sections and permissive to a limited degree in others. This afternoon mention was made of the bank in New Zealand. May I point out that section 10 of the new bank act of New Zealand, a copy of which I hold in my hand, states:
It shall be the general function of the reserve bank, within the limits of its powers, to give effect as far as may be to the monetary policy of the government, as communicated to it from time to time by the Minister of Finance. For this purpose, and to the end that the economic and social welfare of New Zealand may be promoted and maintained, the bank shall regulate and control credit and currency in New Zealand, the transfer of moneys to or from New Zealand, and the disposal of moneys that are derived from the sale of any New Zealand products and for the time being are held overseas.
In other words the government of New Zealand has taken some effective steps at least to endeavour to deliver the producers of that dominion from the control of the international financiers whom the Prime Minister considers, according to one of the speeches to which he alluded this afternoon, responsible for a great many of the difficulties which exist in the world to-day.
As I said at the outset, Mr. Speaker, I do not propose to speak at any great length, but I want to make one point abundantly clear. I believe that this afternoon I speak not only for the little group with which I am associated but for many hundreds, probably thousands, of people who are associated with the party which elected the right hon. Prime Minister of Canada. I believe further that if the speech delivered by the Prime Minister this afternoon, explaining his many speeches made in this house and throughout the country, had been made prior to the election of October 14, 1935, there would not be as many

hon. gentlemen sitting opposite as there are to-day. Again and again during that campaign I met men who said: "We are going to support the Liberal candidate because we believe that the government of Canada, if Liberal, will take over the banking system and give us national control of currency and credit." That inference was drawn, to a large extent, from what was said by the hon. member for Van-couver-Burrard, who campaigned in the province of Saskatchewan. It was drawn also, if I may say so, from many quotations from the speeches of hon. gentlemen who campaigned in Saskatchewan in 1934. May I add that while it had nothing to do with the provincial government it was an effective campaign from the point of view of the provincial Liberal party in that province. A year later, those seeds then sown having flourished and produced fruit, that fruit was garnered by some of the hon. gentlemen who sit on the other side of this house. So I say that if the speech delivered by the right hon. gentleman this afternoon in this chamber had been made prior to October 14 last the Canadian people would have had a much clearer idea of exactly where the Liberal government of Canada was going to stand if elected.
