speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section 3-To whom allowances paid.

Mr. Chairman, I regret that I cannot agree with the minister on this section. I believe that he enjoys the confidence of the returned men of Canada; I know he has done good work for them over a period of many years, and I hope he will be spared to do the same for them for many years to come.
Hear, hear.

Although I am a member of the opposition, it is my intention to cooperate with the minister in every way possible in dealing with the soldier problems as they arise from time to time during the life of this eighteenth parliament. However,
3820
War Veterans' Allowance Act

on this particular section we have been obliged to agree to disagree. This is the section setting out the class of veterans who are eligible for assistance under the War Veterans' Allowance Act. In my opinion this is the most important section of the three bills, Nos. 26, 27, 28, which have been before the house at this session, dealing with soldier problems. I say that it is the most important section because it is the only one under which help can be given now, without any delay, to a considerable body of returned men who are burnt out, men who are really unemployable.
Bill No. 26, to amend the Pension Act, is of course important, because after all the pensioner will always be entitled to first consideration. His disabilities are directly attributable to service, and for that reason, I repeat, he is entitled to first consideration. However, Bill No. 26, as passed by this parliament, gives direct help only to a very limited group of pensioners and their dependents. The main object of Bill No. 26 was to simplify the administration of the Pension Act and to achieve a certain measure of finality. Speaking of finality, I believe that new problems will arise from time to time, and I do not think we can expect the Pension Act to stand without amendment because such new problems as they arise will have to be met by amendments to the act. So much for Bill No. 26.
Bill No. 28 is also important because it provides for the setting up of a veterans' assistance commission. We hope that eventually it will lead to the employment of a great many returned men who are at the present time out of work but who are employable. I wish to distinguish clearly in my remarks between the employable returned man and the unemployable returned man. I say that Bill No. 28 should be of assistance to the employable returned man who at the present time is out of work, but if the members of the committee will refer to Bill No. 28, section 6, they will see that the key words of that bill are "investigate and report," which means that no immediate result can be expected even for the employable returned man. The bill as I see it cannot be of assistance directly to the returned man who is unemployable.
To come to the third bill, Bill No. 27, which we are now considering, my submission is that it is the one bill of the three which will be of any help to the returned man who is unemployable. Speaking for myself alone, I am afraid that the particular section now before the committee, even as it has been amended, will not meet the need. In order
{Mr. Green.]
to explain that statement, I must review the present provisions of the War Veterans' Allowance Act. It was passed in 1930 and has never been amended. The act was passed to benefit the front line man who is defined as a veteran who served in a theatre of actual war. Although there is also provision made for the small pensioner who did not serve in a theatre of actual war but served in England or Canada, the act was primarily intended to benefit the man who served in a theatre of actual war. A returned man must be without means to be eligible for the allowance; he is allowed an income of only S125 per annum if single; if he receives an income larger than that, the difference is taken away from his war veterans' allowance; if he is a married man he is allowed an income of $250 per annum, and in either case he is allowed an interest in his home of a value not over S2,000.
Practically all applicants for war veterans' allowance are returned men who are on relief or who are faced with the necessity of going on relief. I cannot make that point too clear. These men are being largely supported by the government at the present time. The War Veterans' Allowance Act was intended for the benefit of the pre-aged and burnt-out man, the man who is really unemployable. At the present time the allowance is paid to only two classes of veterans: first, those over sixty years of age and, second, those who are permanently unemployable by reason of physical or mental disability. A man may receive a maximum of $20 per month if single or $40 per month if married. No matter how many children he may have he cannot get more than $40 per month. This is not as much as a man could receive on relief in certain cities, but the evidence given before the pension committee was to the effect that the returned man preferred to be under the War Veterans' Allowance Act as he considered he could accept the benefits under that act and still hold his head high. This fact should be kept in mind by hon. members of this committee.
As I have said before, this act has been in force for six years without amendment, but experience has shown beyond question that there are many men under sixty years of age who cannot prove themselves to be permanently unemployable-I make no complaint with reference to those over sixty years of age-but there are many men under sixty years of ago who cannot prove themselves to be permanently unemployable and

3S21
War Veterans' Allowance Act
yet actually they are pre-aged and burnt out and really unemployable. This fact was admitted by the chairman of the war veterans' allowance committee when he appeared before the pension committee, and it was pointed out time and again by representatives of the soldier organizations. There can be no question that this class of returned men are not being provided for at the present time.
The soldier organizations had two suggestions to offer to remedy this defect. One suggestion was that the age limit of sixty years now in the act should be reduced to fifty-five years; in other words, that there should be a general Lowering of the age limit from sixty years to fifty-five years. The other suggestion was that the definition "permanently unemployable" should be changed to "industrially unemployable" without any age limitation whatever. What section 3 of this bill does is to make a very restricted provision for the returned man between the ages of fifty-five and sixty years. This section sets up a new classification and if the bill is passed we shall then have a third group eligible for the war veterans' allowance defined as follows:

or having served in a theatre of actual war, has attained the age of fifty-five years and is, in the opinion of the board, incapable of maintaining himself because of disability, pre-ageing and general unfitness.
The committee will notice that the qualifications necessary for a man to obtain an allowance under this new classification are that he must be between the ages of fifty-five and sixty years and be incapable of maintaining himself by reason of disability, pre-ageing and general unfitness. The word "or" is not used there; the man must be incapable by reason of all three, disability, preageing and general unfitness. It will be noticed that a wide discretion is given to the board; an applicant does not get an allowance as a matter of right; the allowance is confined to veterans who served in a theatre of actual war and of course they must be without means.
My criticism is that this classification is too narrow as it overlooks the veteran below fifty-five years of age who is burnt out and unemployable. The only provision made for such a man is found in a recommendation in the report of the pension committee, which reads as follows:
Your committee also recommends that the veterans' assistance commission to be appointed under the provisions of Bill No. 28 make an investigation into the position of those veterans under the age of 55 years who are by reason of disability, pre-ageing and general unfitness, incapable of maintaining themselves.
This means that those unemployable veterans who are under fifty-five years of age will have to wait for a report from the veterans' assistance commission. No action can be taken until next year, and perhaps even later. In the meantime this class of returned men are on relief with the government paying most of the cost. They are competing in the labour market, sometimes with their own sons. If they are over fifty years of age there is very little chance that they will ever get work again. I suggest to the minister that the proper thing to do would be to provide for this group in the new classification. The range of the new classification is not wide enough to cover these cases. There should have been no age limit or at any rate the group should have included veterans aged from fifty to fifty-five years. If this change were made I believe there would be more chance of getting some permanency in the act and it would go a long way toward meeting the need which obviously is not met by this section.
I think a word should be said for the soldier representatives who appeared before the pension committee. Just a few days ago we saw in the newspapers that the American treasury was sending out truck loads of bonds to American veterans. In contrast there was not the slightest suggestion of high pressure methods being used by our Canadian soldier representatives when they appeared before the pension committee. They presented carefully prepared briefs in a business-like way and I think all members of the pension committee will agree that the representatives who appeared before them were a credit to the returned soldier body of Canada.
In conclusion, I should like to remind the committee of a fact sometimes forgotten. The great majority of returned men have been fortunate enough to fit themselves into the life of the nation; they are bearing their share of all burdens just as are their fellow-Canadians and they are asking nothing of the nation for themselves. But they do ask and ask most earnestly that their comrades who were disabled or who are burnt out should receive reasonable assistance and continued sympathy from the people of Canada.

This section, to my ignorant layman's mind, constitutes two distinct conditions. One is that of the man who has attained the age of sixty, or if he is under that, apparently, because it says:
-or is, in the opinion of the board, permanently unemployable by reason of physical or mental disability.
War Veterans' Allowance Act

And the word "veteran" means a man who has been in a theatre of war. So that the first part of the section is a continuation of the present condition. Then the alternative is:
-or having served in a theatre of actual war.
I do not think there is any necessity for this; if he is a veteran he must have served in a theatre of war.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: The original act provided that the beneficiaries should be either those who had received pension or had served in a theatre of actual war, so that it was possible for a man who had served only in Canada or in England and had 'obtained a pension to come under the provisions of the War Veterans' Allowance Act. That is carried out in the first part of the .section we are discussing. As regards the other point, persons who are now in receipt of pension and who do not comply with the conditions with respect to service in an actual theatre of war shall not be entitled to receive benefits under the act.
Unless such a man has been in a theatre of actual war.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: Yes.

The other point is this. The alternative provision in the case of a man of the age of sixty is that he must be permanently unemployable, and that is a very difficult thing to prove because the board always trots out an elevator and says that if he is not able to do the work to which he has been accustomed all his life he can at any rate run an elevator. The fact that there is not an elevator within 200 miles makes no difference. The minister realizes, of course, that it is difficult to handle such a case. He is, therefore, going to improve matters so far as the man of fifty-five is concerned by making the requisite disability take the form of being incapable of maintaining himself because of disability, pre-ageing and general unfitness. I would rather have seen the word "or" inserted instead of "and" before the words "general unfitness." It appears to me that the man of fifty-five is in a preferential position to the man of sixty. If he is fifty-four he has to prove that he is permanently unemployable by reason of physical disability, but if he is fifty-five he can get past by proving general disability and pre-ageing. Preferential treatment is given to the man of fifty-five. Why not leave out the words "fifty-five" and let the man prove disability, pre-ageing and general unfitness, the age being below sixty? If that were done it would apply to men of fifty-four or fifty-two.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: That is the point which was raised by the hon. gentleman (Mr. Green) who preceded my hon. friend from Comox-Alberni. The difference as between certain members of the committee was this. The majority of the members thought that since we were creating a special class it was very difficult for us to go below fifty-five. As a matter of fact, there is a potential number of 33,000 men who could apply as being between fifty-five and sixty, and if you bring the age limit down to fifty under the same circumstances there is a potential of 88,000, indicating, as my hon. friend recognizes, that soldiers are getting older as time goes on. In view of the fact that this was creating a new class it was thought well to experiment in it before embarking very largely upon any plan in this direction.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
I know quite well that there is, both under the Pension Act and in connection with the War Veterans' Allowance Act, a very large number of cases that are

War Veterans' Allowance Act
really hard, deserving the utmost sympathy of every member of the house, but I believe there is an old adage that says that hard cases make bad law. It would be impossible by legislation to cover all the cases that are meritorious in themselves and that attract our sympathy.
But there is precedent in this case.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: When the War Veterans' Allowance Act was first introduced it was intended to look after soldiers only. It was only under pressure by members of the committee of that day that it was decided to look after the wives of ex-soldiers. This is a provision to take care of burnt-out ex-soldiers themselves. There has been a tendency ever since the act was passed to extend it to everybody, to children and adopted children, and to carry on the allowance for the wife after the beneficiary's death. As a matter of compromise and in order that something should be done for the wife, the law provided that she should receive an allowance for twelve months following her husband's death. Pressure is now being brought to bear to continue this during the lifetime of the wife, and doubtless after that there will be further pressure to continue it during the lifetime of the children. So far as I am concerned, I think this is good legislation. It has served its purpose; it has met with the approval of all sections of the country, and personally I should be very reluctant to change the principle upon which it was based.

I entirely concede everything the minister has said with regard to the merits of the legislation; I think it is the best in the world. But I do not think he entirely answered the point I made. There is precedent for what I suggested. I am merely asking that the same principle be applied to the burnt-out man as to the military man, and I do not think the number of cases would be excessive. I believe there are very few. This legislation is said to be intended for the burnt-out man, who is unable to work; that is the general acceptation. But I am quoting a case-and there must be very few- of a man who is permanently and entirely bedridden, who cannot turn in his bed without assistance, and who has no wife to help him.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: What is his age?

He is under the age of sixty, but he is qualified because he is burnt out and unable to help himself, and ordinarily he would get $40, but because it is his daughter instead of his wife who is attending him she is unable to draw that allowance. We have
a precedent under the military pensions regulations, so that to make provision for such a case would not start a new precedent, nor would it involve any great expense if the same conditions were to apply to such a case as apply to military cases. I would not have the minister think that in pressing him in this matter I fail to appreciate the benefits of this act. I think it is the best legislation of its kind in the world. I would not even ask at the moment that the age should be reduced to fifty. I think when that is done we should also reduce the old age pension age to sixty-five. But in the case I have mentioned, and in the very few isolated cases of the same kind that must occur-and the minister's officials will know how few they are-I ask that an allowance should be made for what is called total helplessness, and that where the man is drawing only $20, he should be given an extra $20 to help him pay an assistant.

I wish to say a word about this particular section, as I come from a district called Broadview, referred to yesterday by the Minister of Justice. This is the riding which has such a broad point of view that it sent more troops to the front than did any other riding in Canada.
Except Davenport.

I used to represent Northwest Toronto, in which was Christie Street hospital. My present riding has the most men who are affected by this particular clause and who are fifty-five years old being bom in 1881, about four years before the northwest rebellion, when troops to the number of three battalions, composed to the extent of seventy-five per cent of Toronto men, went to the northwest to save this country from disintegration. The men who served in that campaign were treated disgracefully by this parliament. Many of them died without a pension. I was struck by the contrast when I was in Washington recently and saw how readily a bill was passed, involving hundreds of millions of dollars, for the benefit of former members of the American expeditionary force. Many who never saw the front lines. Yet, compared with the achievements of the troops who went from Canada, the accomplishments of the American army were small and insignificant.
I commend the work that has been done by this particular committee. It is glorious work, well done as far as it went. Consider what this country has done for some of the people who stayed at home. Take the DuPont corporation; think of the hundreds of millions of dollars which it made during the war and after. One of its Canadian officials, a man who did not go to the war, has been appointed
War Veterans' Allowance Act

chairman of the employment commission. I refer to Mr. Purvis, head of the DuPont in Canada. What did the returned men get as lompared to him?
This particular bill refers to unemployment. Every day I see men who went to the front and served there in the battle for civilization, and it is humiliating to me, as one of those who presided over a great city during the war, to note the present condition of these men and their children in distress. I do not know what they would have done but for the Poppy Day fund and the women's organization connected with Christie Street hospital. I see the children of these veterans on the streets wearing second-hand clothing; I see the wives with second-hand baby carriages. Such things are a disgrace to the people of this country.
Once again I commend the good work that this committee has done. The present minister does not need to have sitting beside him a schoolmaster when he is passing the items of this bill; I can give him that credit, anyway. I note that the purpose of the amendment in section 3 is to provide that in specially meritorious cases, such as preageing and general unfitness, a veteran may be classified as permanently unemployable on reaching the age of fifty-five instead of sixty, which is the age mentioned in the first part of section 4. I might remark for the benefit of the Minister of Justice that next Sunday there will be about 30,000 troops assembled in the Broadview riding, at Riverdale park for their annual service, but that is a broad place. I take a broad view when I am dealing with any question. But he promises in a bill to do something, and does nothing. These 30,000 men will meet in Riverdale park. I do not often go down there, because I never appeal to the soldier vote; I am not a soldier and so am not in a class to talk to the men who went to the front and gave service. But I see these men on the streets every day, and I visit their homes. Some of them, because of the way in which they are treated by the people of this country, cannot to-day send their children to high school.
Christie Street hospital was in my riding. When the war closed the military hospital was just a factory; this country put its wounded men into an old base hospital on Gerrard street, which as mayor of the city, I refused to allow to be used. It was not good enough for civilians, and was closed; why was it considered good enough to be occupied by men who served at the front? Some of them were supposed to be put into the Toronto gaol, but I said on behalf of the city that,

by the grace of God, no man who had served in France and Flanders would ever be put into a Toronto gaol for one small breach of military regulations, and we refused them the use of this old building. I speak only as a civilian, but I see these men in Christie Street hospital, away on the top floor. Why should they be there, serving what amounts to a life sentence? For they are sentenced by this high court of parliament to a life sentence three or four floors up in the Christie Street hospital. I am not criticizing those who look after them, the nurses and others, for they are a wonderful lot of people.
Persons who are fifty-five years of age should be taken off the labour market altogether. In the meanwhile it seems to me that better jobs could be found for some of these men. All the jobs the returned soldiers in this country get are pick and shovel jobs. I am not criticizing the present government, or the minister, who served with a Toronto battalion at t'he front, and who is admired and respected by the exservice men of Toronto. But I do not think ,the amendment goes 'half far enough, considering what these men have done, and what was done at Washington. The United States did not vote a few millions; as every banking house knows, the amount they granted runs into billions. Yet some of t'he men who are receiving this money never left t'heir native shores. The 347th regiment of the United States army, which came from Seattle, went through Toronto. I saw other battalions also, some of them from the states and some never did a day's fighting; yet the men are getting pensions and allowances and need do no work after they are forty. They never fired a pinwheel, a. firecracker or a skyrocket on behalf of the President of the United States.
I desire to commend this section, although, when I consider what this dominion has wasted, in natural resources of soil and forest and mine, to American millionaires and their friends, I think the section does not go far enough. The farmers, the Ontario Drury government, gave away a whole principality half the size of Belgium, to an American millionaire, Mr. Backus.
When a returned soldier comes home, and is fifty-five years of age, do you think he is 100 per cent efficient? If the whole 245 members of the present House of Commons were transported to Belgium and France; if they had to sleep, with hardly anything to eat for three or four nights at a time, away below the ground, as the present able young minister and colleagues of his on both sides

War Veterans' Allowance Act
of the 'house had to do; if members went over there and suffered the privations and human tribulations and trials of every kind that these men went through, and then came back from the front with no better conditions facing their children than are experienced by many of our returned men to-day, they would realize the position of many men in my constituency. When the children go to high school, although the teachers, many of whom are returned soldiers, are friendly to them, they cannot afford any longer to pay their fees. The result is the boys of the family go to new Ontario, and are sent to gaol because they are vagrants. I brought in a bill and appealed to the House of Commons; yet not one member supported it.
I saw these conditions while I was an officer of the municipality for fourteen or fifteen years, and I see them now as a member of parliament. I do not care about the race or religion of these returned men; I am trying to help them. I have never seen anything like the suffering they and their families are undergoing at the present time. I have visited their homes; I have seen them in rags and in want. I do not know what they would do if it were not for the Poppy Day fund. Every day in the daily newspapers of Toronto I see advertisements asking for second-hand baby carriages, secondhand socks, second-hand shoes and secondhand clothing of all kinds. This is a disgrace to the people of this country. I want to commend the government, or rather the committee, for the work they have done, but when I see one of the DuPont crowd appointed as chairman of the employment commission and at the same time see the men waiking around the streets of Toronto, I think this is a disgrace. The city of Toronto cannot carry the whole burden, as it has done in the past. To the 245 members of this House of Commons I say: Go to Christie Street hospital; see the rooms and wards up on the top floor, where the men never get a breath of fresh air. See the wifes and children of these veterans, some of them five and six years of age. I say that this is a disgrace to the people of Canada. We talk about sending a few men to the old country. Well, after spending about four and a half million dollars on the League of Nations, which gets nowhere, the government cannot afford to send thirty-five members of this house over to the reunion at Vimy Ridge. Vimy Ridge cost the city of Toronto 2,000 men and $2,000,000 in insurance which was carried on the men by the city. I started to
help recruit tihe 75th battalion; it raised 16,000 men, of whom more than 1,200 fell at Vimy Ridge. I have visited the homes of some of the members of this battalion, and what I have seen there makes me ashamed to be a Canadian. Upon my word I am ashamed to be a member of the House of Commons of Canada when I see the conditions that exist in my constituency. I know of one case, a woman whose husband might have had a good job in this country to-day, an educated woman, who has to take in washing in order to support her small children who are attending a high school in my riding. I protest against that sort of thing.
I may talk too mueh sometimes; I hope all talk for this session will be over tomorrow at midnight, but I do not think we can talk too much about these matters. I knew the minister during and before the war, as a hockey player, and I want to thank him for what he has done. Both he and the young minister from British Columbia came to Christie Street hospital and saw the conditions that exist on the upper floor of that institution. I hope the Minister of Finance may find it possible to release a few thousand dollars in order to relieve the condition of these men who have been sentenced to life in an institution where there is not a breath of air and where the thermometer may stand at 96 or 97 degrees. If we gave these men full pay we could not begin to compensate them for what they have done and what they have gone through. What is the situation in the United States? There are generals and brigadier-generals around Washington getting full pensions though they never set foot in France. And colonels! They have about 367 colonels in Kentucky who have never fired anything more dangerous than a pinwheel, a firecracker or a sky-rocket, who have never been outside the United States and who also are drawing full pensions.

The war veterans' allowance board, however, has ruled, in pursuance of an opinion given by the Justice department, that irrespective of whether the man himself served in the theatre of war and irrespective of whether or not he has all the other qualifications, he cannot receive a war veterans' allowance unless his unit served in a theatre of war.
I took occasion to lay before the committee one concrete case which I believe is illustrative of some twenty-five or thirty cases in this country. A man was assigned the job of non-commissioned conducting officer. His job was to conduct troops through the dangerous channels from the base in England to the place in France where they joined some other unit. The men who did that work were subjected to the hazards of war both by sea and on land just as much as those who served in almost any of the transport services. But because a man was attached to a unit which was situated in England, even though he may be qualified on all other grounds under this act, it is said that he cannot obtain a war veteran's allowance. I suggested to the committee that since that interpretation of the definition contained in the act seemed clearly contrary to the plain reading of the act, the necessary amendments should be made to clarify the situation. I see the committee has not seen fit to recommend such an amendment. As far as I am concerned I merely desire every member of this committee to realize that the definition in this act does not mean one who served in a theatre of war; under a ruling or interpretation by the Justice department, no matter what service a man rendered he is still out of luck unless his unit actually served in France, thus coming within the definition of service in a theatre of war.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
The case presented by my hon. friend is quite familiar to me. As the hon. gentleman says, quite a number of claims -probably ten or fifteen-have been made for war veterans' allowance by men who went on a Cook's tour to France or served as conducting officers. The war veterans' allowance board consulted the Department of Justice some time in 1932, and the department ruled that such men, though they actually did set foot on the soil of France and under a strict interpretation of the definition of a theatre of actual war could be looked upon as having served in a theatre of actual war, could not be considered under the War Veterans' Allowance Act because they had not been attached to a unit situated in France.
The same ruling was given, I am informed by the militia department in connection with the medals which were issued to those who saw service in France and in connection with

various other matters having reference to military service. If my hon. friend wants my opinion may I say that I would be glad to discuss this matter with the law officers of the crown. I think there is a great deal to be said in favour of the interpret ation of the act given by the hon. member. But there was no amendment which we could make. As he himself has said, the act is quite clear. "Theatre of actual war" means in the case of military or air forces the zone of the allied armies on the continents of Europe, Asia and Africa. Well, the person on whose behalf my hon. friend speaks did serve in one of the armies of His Majesty in a zone of actual war on the continent of Europe. That is quite clear; there could be no argument about it. It would not have been possible to amend the act to cover it, because it is there in the act as I read it. But in this individual case there is a ruling, which I believe has been in existence since the war, that conducting officers, those who have been on Cook's tours and who just went around France to visit the trenches, were not to be considered as people who served in the theatre of actual war. I do not think it is within my jurisdiction or part of my duty as a minister to order the war veterans' allowance committee to issue an allowance. I would think I was acting in an arbitrary manner and in a manner parliament did not intend a minister to act if I were to take that duty upon myself.
Very properly, I believe, the chairman and members of the war veterans' allowance committee referred the disputed point to the Department of Justice. I have nothing further to say on the matter, except that we could not meet the hon. member by making an amendment. I could not meet him by issuing an instruction to the war veterans' allowance committee to accede to his wishes. I think he has a perfectly sound legal argument to make before the Department of Justice, and I wish him well when he makes his argument.
The hon. member for York South has said that the section refers to a person whose unit served in France.
No, that is what the Department of Justice says it means.
It says "any former member who served in a theatre of actual war."

Yes, but the Department of Justice says that it does not mean that. Hon. members will see the position into which we are getting at this time. My hon. friend, whom I shall refrain from commending as a lawyer -because at the moment he happens to agree with me-says that to him it is just as plain as it is to me that the law means what I say it

War Veterans' Allowance Act
means, and what the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill) and any person who reads it must conclude it means. Here we have before parliament a responsible minister of the government who says: "Plainly that is what the law means, but I cannot instruct the Department of Justice not to thwart the law and to say that it is something other than parliament says it is. I cannot instruct the war veterans' allowance committee." I do not think any blame attaches to the board. Being confronted with a case they submitted it to the Department of Justice. They could not set themselves up as interpreters of the law and give to that law an interpretation different from that given by the Department of Justice.
I shall not take the time of the committee to deal with the statement made by the minister with respect to Cook's tours. If some other members will keep this debate going long enough to let me go to my office and get my files I could show the minister that the person to whom I was referring was not on a Cook's tour.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: Perhaps the hon. member misunderstood me. I spoke about conducting officers and people who went on what we called Cook's tours. As my hon. friend must know, so that they would not return to Canada without having at least set foot in France and been in the front line, a large number of officers managed to arrange what were called Cook's tours. They spent a week or a few days with the battalion, and then returned home. If my hon. friend's-interpretation of the act is accepted, then certainly those men would be entitled to war veterans' allowance and to the same military medals as those men who served in the front line. It must be remembered, too, that the conducting officers did not have an extremely dangerous job. In fact they had what might be called "cushy" jobs; I do not want a better one in the next war.	.
I want to say at the outset that I am very sorry if I misinterpreted the remarks of the minister, or if I said anything that would injure him-

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: No; you did not.

I may have misunderstood him. I want to say, however, that some of these non-commissioned conducting officers had just as hazardous occupations as many others who are drawing pensions, and I am not referring to the miserable pittance obtained under war veterans' allowance; I refer to pensions. Conducting officers did run a hazard, if they had to cross the English channel they were on a hazardous voyage.
If they had to make trips from the landing point in France to the base line of action, they ran a hazard; they ran the hazard of shell fire, and the hazard of bombs from aeroplanes. I do not wish to get into a discussion of that kind, but I know of no way of preventing the Department of Justice from saying the law is what parliament says it is not, unless parliament changes the wording to make it so plain that the Department of Justice cannot possibly say that that is not what the statute means.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
I have no objection to
referring the case back to the Department of Justice, if my hon. friend so desires. I believe he himself discussed it with the law officers of the crown, if I am not mistaken.
No.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: I have no objection to referring the case back for decision.
As we are confronted with a situation wherein the Department of Justice has given a ruling which appears to be contrary to the spirit of the act-

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: I would not say it was contrary to the spirit of the act. Quite frankly I am willing to tell the committee I do not think it was ever the spirit of the act to have a condition whereby conducting officers would come under it, and I will take the responsibility for making that statement.

The spirit of the act would certainly refer to those who served in the theatre of actual war. Could we not say, "who served in the theatre of actual war," and exclude those people, who, as the minister says, were on Cook's tours? We could make a provision whereby a trip to the lines not exceeding so many days would not count. Surely it is possible for us to frame a definition in such a way as to meet the objection of the Department of Justice and still be fair to the cases about which the hon. member for York South has spoken. That should be within the legal ability of the minister and his associates; surely they could draw up a section which would be proof against the opinion of the Department of Justice.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
About how many men of sixty are now drawing those allowances, and what was the amount paid last year? With respect to the last point made may I say that I believe the difficulty lies in the word "served." The men to whom the hon. member for York South referred have not served in a theatre of actual war, within the meaning of

the statute. They were there merely as conducting officers, or whatever they may be called, and therefore did not serve within the meaning of that word. Does not the Department of Justice say that?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
The Department of Justice alleges that there must be attachment to a unit. On the other hand I shall have to say this to the hon. member for York South, that certain staff officers could not be said to be attached to units, and yet they no doubt would be qualified for a war veterans' allowance.
With respect to the first point raised by my right hon. friend may I say that there are altogether about 9,000 enjoying war veterans' allowances, and of that number about two-thirds are above the age of sixty and one-third below sixty.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Between fifty-five and sixty?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: No. At the present time the act provides for those who are unable to maintain themselves and have passed the age of sixty. We assume that they are permanently unemployable if they have reached sixty.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: That has been the law for over five years.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
Since 1930. If they are below sixty years and can establish that they are permanently unemployable on account of mental or physical disability, they come under the act.
The present section which is being proposed to the committee creates a new class. The war veterans' allowance committee, in travelling throughout the country, found that there was a large number of men who were not quite sixty years of age and not quite physically unemployable. They are fairly well recognizable problem oases, and it is to cover these cases that we are introducing this amendment. It is for those over fifty-five years of age, most of them problem cases, who cannot obtain a doctor's certificate that they are permanently disabled. Most of these cases are approaching sixty; they are between fifty-five and sixty, and it was thought we should create a class between fifty-five and sixty years of age of those who were disabled, pre-aged, infirm, and who, while not quite permanently unemployable, yet were incapable of maintaining themselves. It was very difficult to express in legal language the thought that was in the mind of the members of the war veterans' allowance committee, but they were given a discretion to take in a certain number of men who undoubtedly should be looked after in some way.

My hon. friends who have spoken have suggested that we should take in all those down to fifty years of age. The average age of our soldiers is now approximately forty-seven, and to adopt that suggestion would really mean an unemployment relief measure. This act, I submit, was never intended as an unemployment relief measure for soldiers. It was an extension of the principle on which every government and every soldiers' committee has acted since these committees have been studying this question. The principle is that no one is entitled to a pension unless he has a disability which was incurred on or due to service. That is to say, disability due to sendee is the determining factor whether he shall get a pension or not.
Then, in 1930, it was found that there was a large number of men who could not possibly establish their right to pension, so this parliament established a species of presumption that they were over-aged, burnt out, and parliament made that age ten years less than that provided under the old age pension legislation. They said that a man of sixty who served in a theatre of actual war might be presumed, on account of the hardships he had undergone and on account of the life of the trenches, to be burnt out, and therefore they said that he would get an allowance. Then they said that if a man were permanently unemployable on account of some physical or mental disability which he could not trace to service, he too, if he were ill, if he were indigent, should be entitled to an allowance.
Now it has been found that the words "permanently unemployable" did not cover a sufficiently large number of men, and certain service associations and certain of my hon. friends felt that we should perhaps say "industrially unemployable." I think every hon. member will immediately understand that that means unemployment insurance; in other words, that would have taken in every soldier, every man who put on a uniform, the moment he became unemployed. I do not think that was ever the intention of parliament, and certainly it was not the intention of parliament when this act was introduced. We have gone a long way in saying that we would endeavour to take care of the problem cases.
I do not know that I should discuss the question of cost, but my right hon. friend has asked me certain questions. With respect to the number of persons who are now in the enjoyment of war veterans' allowance, those sixty years of age and over number 6,194, and the amount expended during the last fiscal year on that class was $1,892,672; under sixty years of age and permanently unemployable

War Veterans' Allowance Act
on account of physical disabilities, the number is 2,626, and the amount expended $887,599; making a total for the last fiscal year of 8,820 persons profiting by the allowance, at an expenditure of $2,780,271. We have asked the house-and the estimate has been passed-for an amount of $3,200,000 this year.
Under this new amendment we are asking that an amount of $200,000 be inserted in the supplementary estimates to cover the balance of the fiscal year, making it roughly $300,000 additional a year, taking in the class from fifty-five to sixty years of age. I have no means of knowing how much more it would be if we took in the class from fifty to sixty years of age, but I think it is at least fair to assume that there would be at least as many, and the proposal made by my hon. friends in that regard would add to the bill something like $600,000 a year. The total of war veterans' allowances is now accelerating at the rate of $400,000 a year, without the provisions of this amendment, and I am informed that the amount next year will be $650,000 more than it was last year. Perhaps the committee would be interested in getting some of the figures. The amount of war veterans' allowances paid in 1933 was $2,224,000; in 1934, $2,500,000; in 1935, $2,800,000; in 1936, $3,200,000; in 1937, $3,500,000. Now I jump to 1940, when the estimated amount will be $4,700,000; 1945, $6,300,000; 1950, $9,174,000; 1951.	$10,090,000;	1955,	$11,269,000;	1956,
$11,602,000; 1957, $11,809,000, and in that year we would have reached the estimated peak of expenditure if no change was being made in the War Veterans' Allowance Act. Under this legislation we are accelerating the total amount paid by at least from $200,000 to $300,000 a year; the peak will probably be reached a great deal earlier, probably some time in the early 1950's, and I say that without having any figure before me. The amount which will be expended over a period of ten years will be considerable.
Had we accepted the proposal made by certain soldier organizations and others outside, that the age limit be reduced to fifty-five without any qualifications, within ten years the estimated additional expenditure would have been $25,974,000, and had we accepted the proposal to bring the age down to fifty, the estimated additional expenditure would have been $46,058,000. That is one of the reasons why it was not considered advisable to jump at once into a very large additional expenditure. Besides, the war veterans' assistance commission, if it is to accomplish anything-and I hope it will-will endeavour to find means of employment for the 30,000 to 40,000 exsoldiers who are not now in receipt of a pension or in receipt of war veterans' allowance, but are entitled to some consideration on the part of the people of Canada.
Mr. BENNETT; That was mentioned in the Hyndman report.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
My right hon. friend has
mentioned the Hyndman report. As he knows, the Hyndman commission's report attracted a great deal of attention and a great deal of support throughout the country. The commission reported as follows:
To enact that a man who is out of work at the age of 50 or 55 is permanently unemployable would be to depart from the intention of the act and would virtually convert any benefits under that act into general service pensions. A large majority of those who are under 60 years of age and who are out of work, are so situated because of economic and not physical conditions, and it is felt by your committee that the recommendations contained in this report will, in large measure, provide the temporary assistance requird by those for whom employment cannot readily be found, without branding them as unemployable for the rest of their lives.
We have given very close and earnest consideration to all these requests, and are constrained to the view that it would be unwise to disturb the principle upon which the War Veterans' Allowance Act was based.
In view of the evidence given before this commission which carefully investigated the matter, I believe that anyone who has the real interests of the ex-soldier at heart-had I more time I might go into this more fully- will agree that the committee would be wise to go forward only one step in the direction in which it 'has gone at the present time. Possibly at some future date, should nothing else be done for the unemployed ex-soldier, the parliament of Canada may decide to depart from the principle which it has followed heretofore and to take on its shoulders the charge of all ex-service men in Canada who are not pensioners and who have no service disability. That will be the responsibility of government and of parliament when the time comes to frame such a policy. At the present time I do not feel that we have sufficient information before us and that public opinion has been sufficiently educated to take a step so far in a direction which I think will inevitably not be of benefit to the ex-service man.
Mr. BENNETT; Has the minister concluded that the word "domiciled" in the last line of section 3 is the word that adequately expresses what he has in mind? In law the word "domicile" means a combination of two factors, residence and intention. A man must have residence without any animus revertendi. I am not endeavouring to lecture the committee, but the use of this word is always
War Veterans' Allowance Act

dangerous because it involves great difficulty of proof. It has arisen so frequently in the courts that I wondered whether it was being used synonymously with "residence," or whether or not the minister had in mind the use of the complex term "domicile."

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: After a rather long and fairly checkered career in a sphere not so nonpartisan as that in which we are now in connection with the elections act, I did learn a great deal about the word "domicile." I quite agree with my right hon. friend that that word does not mean residence, far from it, but I am informed that it was in the original act as it was passed in 1930 and is being interpreted by the committee as meaning ordinary residence.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: It is very dangerous in case it gets into a court of law.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: I quite agree.

Mr. Chairman, I wish to
express very briefly my concurrence in the views advanced by the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Green). I join with him and other members of the committee in expressing appreciation of the sympathetic attitude shown by the minister to these problems throughout the entire proceedings of the pension committee. I do not wish to appear to be unduly critical of the section under discussion at the moment as I recognize its value in that it confers benefits upon a certain category of ex-service men. It is an important step towards the solution of an urgent problem. Nevertheless I urged throughout the proceedings of the committee -and I do so again

that this section in its present form does not adequately meet the situation as now defined.
I agree with the minister when he says that the underlying principle of this legislation should not be departed from at this time. I would hesitate to advocate any change .that would convert the War Veterans' Allowance Act into an unemployment relief measure. This act was intended to meet the needs of ex-service men who have suffered a premature breakdown due to the hazard, strain and exposure undergone while on active service. While I recognize the value of the existing legislation, the fact is that men who have not attained the age of sixty years and who are in indigent circumstances cannot obtain the benefits of this legislation unless it can be demonstrated on medical evidence that they are permanently unemployable.
I believe the present classification is unduly restrictive. Before entitlement may be established under this section, a man must demonstrate that he is fifty-five, that he served

in a theatre of actual war; that he is now incapable of maintaining himself by reason of disability, pre-ageing and general unfitness. In my opinion that seriously restricts the benefits of this section,. I am glad the members of the committee, the minister and the chairman of the war veterans' allowance committee have found this formula. I think in the words "incapable of maintaining himself because of disability, pre-ageing and general unfitness" we have a safe formula which may be applied to other age groups without in any sense disturbing the principle of the act. I submit, as I have submitted on previous occasions, that the evidence given before the committee proved very clearly that there are a number of problem cases in the age groups below fifty-five years which should be. provided for. I submit further that it is in the public interest, as well as in the interests .of these men, that their needs should be met promptly. The more promptly they are met, the greater will be the possibility of some measure of rehabilitation. It should be borne in mind that when a man becomes employable the war veterans' allowance committee 'has the power to strike him off the list. I think we have a perfectly safe formula to deal with these oases. However exhaustive may be the inquiries of the war veterans' assistance committee, there are certain clearly defined categories of ex-service men who are uemployable to-day and for whom no provision has been made nor can otherwise be made.
I feel that the minister is unduly alarmed at the possibility of assuming additional responsibility. It has been suggested that the recruiting field for applications may be to some extent larger in the age group of fifty to fifty-five years than it is in the group of fifty-five to sixty years, but it was shown before the committee that the ratio of those who might qualify was considerably lower in the age groups below fifty-five years. I submit that this formula may be safely extended to other age groups below fifty-five years, and in all justice it should be done now. If it is thought reasonable to assume some responsibility with regard to those between fifty-five and sixty years of age, I think there is at least equal justice for our conferring upon the board discretionary power to deal with these cases of breakdown due to disability, pre-ageing and general unfitness in the case of men below fifty-five years of age. I think this discretion can safely be left with the board.
I feel it my duty to say a word in appreciation of the very capable administration that has been given this legislation during the last

War Veterans' Allowance Act
five or six years. I can testify personally as to the remarkable degree of confidence which the war veterans' allowance committee enjoys among ex-service men generally throughout Canada. While the opinion prevails that this amendment is all that should be undertaken at this time, I most earnestly hope that the act will be interpreted in such a way as to implement the recommendations of the committee. The phrase "permanently unemployable" should be interpreted in the broadest possible sense. I also hope that at the earliest possible moment the minister will secure from the veterans' assistance commission a special report dealing with the plight of those veterans who are incapable of maintaining themselves at this time and for whom no provision has been made in the amended bill.

I wish to associate myself with the remarks of the hon. members for Vancouver South (Mr. Green) and Vancouver North (Mr. MacNeil). They have expressed my views far better than I could do so myself and I shall not repeat what they have said. On the resolution leading up to this bill I gave it as my opinion that the dead line should be not fifty-five but fifty years. I held that opinion during the proceedings of the committee and towards the close of the committee's sittings I changed it and came to feel that perhaps that dead line should be swept away altogether. That is my present view. However, having regard to the assurance of the minister that the report of the veterans' assistance commission will be studied very carefully; that the work of that commission may provide for those who are not taken care of in the present legislation, and above all that the door is not closed and that this matter may be reconsidered, and having regard further to the expressed desire of a very considerable body of the men concerned, that no difference of opinion appear in the proceedings of the committee, I allowed my own personal views to fall into the background and concurred in the report of the committee. I feel very strongly that there will be men whose cases will not be met by the provisions of this bill, and if it turns out that they are not provided for by the veterans' assistance commission I wish to make it clear that in voting for this bill I am reserving the right to speak in their interests at another session of parliament.

I think we are all in sympathy with the object of this legislation and with the method adopted to provide for a class of men who are very deserving and
whom perhaps it is difficult to put into any well defined category. It is well recognized that laws should be as certain as possible, and the only objection to this section is the element of uncertainty in it. I sincerely hope, therefore, that the department will be able to make decisions which will clarify the situation and render it easy as a matter of administration for the department and for those who are interested in the returned men to decide whether they fall within the rulings of the department which will afford them relief. The main objection to the section is its uncertainty and the large number of cases which will remain in doubt and which will be subject from time to time to, shall I say, an arbitrary ruling of the department in each particular case.

Would the minister consider changing in the second last line the word "thirty" to "twenty." If we leave it as it stands, thirty years, it means that we are carrying it back nearly forty years. This question arises more often in connection with applications for old age pension, but it arises in this matter as well. You go to some illiterate man or old woman and say that the bureau of statistics will reveal his or her age. But in this case the census must have been taken more than thirty years before the date of the application for information. The first question the bureau will ask is: Where were you when the census was taken. The second question is: What was the name of the registrar or enumerator. An uneducated man who has been travelling around the country for the last forty years has only the vaguest idea where he was in 1901, and very often he will give the wrong place and the wrong name of the enumerator. I have had a good deal of experience in this regard and I know of people who are without pensions to-day because their records cannot be located. 19.	When and where was first public notice given of such order in council?
The reply was, "No information." And then a motion:
C9 Py of all correspondence between the Minister of Railways and Canals, from May 31, 1933. to October 23, 1935, and one or any of the Canadian banks or any railway company, in connection with the guarantee given by the government for the $60,000,000 loan to the Canadian Pacific Railway.
No. 171-D, answer of the Department of Railways and Canals: "No record in this department of any such correspondence."
[The Chairman.]
Now we take the Department of Finance, 171-C:
Copy of all correspondence between the Minister of Finance, from May 31, 1933, to October 23, 1935, and one or any of the Canadian banks or any railway company, in connection with the guarantee given by the government for the $60,000,000 loan to the Canadian Pacific Railway.
1/1-C. The only letters now on file in the Department of Finance with regard to this $60,000,000 loan until the last government left office are: First, letter from Sir Charles Gordon to Mr. Rhodes, December 9, 1933, sending eight agreements executed in duplicate by the eight banks; second, from Mr. Rhodes to Sir Charles Gordon, December 11, 1933, returning one copy each of the eight agreements which he had executed in duplicate; third, from the same to the same, December 12, 1933; fourth, acknowledgment by Sir Charles Gordon, December 13, 1935.
I tell the right hon. leader of the opposition that, if he had acted in the same fashion as the hon. Minister of Finance did, the letters that were written prior to that would be still on file in the Department of Finance.
Mark you, sir;
In the minutes and records of the privy council, did the signatures of the Honourable E. N. Rhodes, then Minister of Finance, and of the Honourable W. A. Gordon, then Minister of Labour, appear for the first time in matters pertaining to the dominion guarantee of the $60,000,000 C.P.R. loan in memorandum of November 28, 1933, to His Excellency the Governor General in Council, for P.C. 2490?
The answer of the privy council is, in return 171-0 of June 12: "Yea." It was the first time that the signature of the hon. Minister of Finance and the hon. Minister of Labour appeared with regard to that transaction.
Now, sir, there is only one matter left. It is with regard to the refunding of the whole thing. The right hon. leader of the opposition has spoken of "wildly extravagant statements" which were not warranted when I said that it was three days after the Canadian Pacific Railway loan was mentioned in the House of Commons by the member for Temiscouata that the whole amount, which was not then due, was paid by the Canadian Pacific Railway. I hope the right hon. leader of the opposition will open his ear and listen to this. It is on Hansard, June 10:
1. Did order in council P.C. 2490 of November 29, 1933, provide for any date of maturity for the repayment of the whole or any part of the $60,000,000 Canadian Pacific Railway loan which was guaranteed by the dominion government?
Answer: "Yes."

none." It is surprising, because the right hon. gentleman was saying that all the time they mentioned the refunding of that loan, and while $12,000,000, one-fifth of the amount, was paid in 1934, there was nothing, according to the record, paid in 1935, the last year he was Prime Minister. Answer:	"Yes." According to what the
right hon. gentleman has said, the answer should have been "No."

Answer: "April 27, 1936." Exactly what I have said. It means that the date the Canadian Pacific Railway loan was mentioned in this house was the very same day the president of that company notified the government that the amount which was due, and even that part which had not yet matured, were to be paid three days later, on May 1. The last question was:
8.	Was the Minister of Finance advised by the chartered banks that the principal amount of the loan together with interest thereon, had been paid on May 1st?
Answer: "Yes."
I shall say no more than that. The case is just as complete as it can be. The first time that the signatures of the hon. Minister of Finance and the hon. Minister of Labour appear is on November 28, 1933, on the memorandum, in spite of the fact that the letter of guarantee was given six months before, on May 31, 1933. Not only that. There are three or four letters in the Department of Finance which were written afterwards by the then Minister of Finance; there is no correspondence in the meantime except
from the then acting Prime Minister and the Prime Minister himself.
I suffered so much some years ago, when I was called twice to order because I had said to the then Minister of Marine that public letters should not be changed into confidential letters, that I am very much surprised that the hon. member for Calgary West, who made so much fuss about the matter at the time, assumed on his own responsibility to take away with him letters that belonged to the state with regard to a guarantee of S60,000,000. That is all, sir.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, we of this side of the house and all those who form the official opposition have always accepted your rulings, I think, with very great respect indeed. Bill No. 100, which we are now discussing, does in one clause refer to agreements with corporations, but I call your attention to the fact that it says:
The governor in council may also enter into agreements with corporations, partnerships, or individuals engaged in industry respecting the expansion of industrial employment.
We all know that the guarantee given to the Canadian Pacific Railway had nothing to do with a guarantee respecting the expansion of industrial employment. With that before my eyes, I nevertheless accepted your ruling and did not attempt to appeal therefrom. But I do say this-and I call your attention to it as the chairman of committees and the deputy speaker of this house-that recently certain questionable interjections in this house have become intolerable.
With respect to these questions that have been asked repeatedly with regard to the Canadian Pacific guarantee, every member of this house and every member of the present government who has knowledge of the facts knows that the guarantee was made in good faith; that it was absolutely above suspicion and that the liability has been repaid so that the treasury has not lost a single dollar on that account. I do not know exactly, but it may be and I believe was the case that there was confidential correspondence for a certain period relating to the proposed arrangements to be made with the banks, several of whom were concerned with this guarantee in favour of the Canadian Pacific Railway. Confidential correspondence was carried on for a time with regard to these matters. But when official action was to be taken, a representation would be made by way of recommendation to His Excellency the Governor in Council, and on that recommendation an order in council would be framed and passed. The

order in council which was so framed and passed is the official document completing the transaction, and the hon. member has no right to call for the confidential communications from day to day in which the final basis of the agreement was developed. I venture to say to the Minister of Finance that even since he came into office this time, and certainly when he was in office before, he had necessarily to have confidential correspondence with many persons interested in public affairs before he finally made his recommendations to council dealing with those matters which were definitely embodied in orders of His Excellency the Governor in Council.
Furthermore, Mr. Chairman, if the Prime Minister were here to-night I am sure he would concede that under an order in council which is passed at the inception of each successive administration the Prime Minister, by order of his colleagues, is given certain exceptional prerogative rights.

And for sixty years or more that order in council has been regarded as confidential. That order in council has never been brought down in this house, but it is an order in council passed by each government on assuming office, giving more or less in detail a statement of the rights and prerogative privileges which the Prime Minister's colleagues confer upon him. More than that, on one occasion I traced back each successive order in council, I think away back to the time of Sir John A. Macdonald, in order to ascertain certain facts which were important with respect to government action at that time. Each administration, with the exception of a slight difference in wording from time to time as new conditions arose, has followed exactly the same form in respect of that order in council. The Prime Minister, or whoever replied to the hon. gentleman, indicated to him that there was an order in council outstanding, the order in council constituting the Bennett administration, if I may so call it, which authorized the right hon. leader of the government of that day to act on behalf and in the name of his colleagues. It is impossible to carry on government unless some person has such authority in case of the temporary absence of some member of the government. That practice has continued to this day, and I suggest that it is quite improper to take from it any undue inference such as has been drawn by the hon. member for Temiseouata to-night.

Further, Mr. Chairman, I do say that I wish you, as chairman, would again consider and review these proceedings of to-night. I accepted your ruling. I did not appeal from it; I thought it better that we should have this tempest now than at another time. But such proceedings render the position of members of this house utterly intolerable, because they surpass the ordinary decencies of debate. When one becomes a member of this house we assume that he will conform to the ordinary dictates of decency and that he will act in a gentlemanly way, and it is with that in mind-

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, some days
ago I gave an undertaking that on or not later than Thursday I would move that the house go into committee of supply in order that we might, take up an item which has been reserved in the estimates of the Department of External Affairs, namely the item relating to Geneva, so that we might have a discussion on foreign affairs. I think it would perhaps serve a useful purpose if, at the outset, the discussion took place in a formal way, and if the debate were to be carried for a time at least with His Honour the Speaker in the chair. Subsequently we could go into committee for any detailed information hon. members may wish to have. If hon. members are agreeable to proceeding in 'that way I would ask for unanimous consent to move that the provision of standing order 28, respecting committee of supply, be suspended for Thursday, June 18 instant, the reason being that on Thursdays Mr. Speaker leaves the chair without question being put. If the motion is
carried I would propose to-morrow, before Mr. Speaker leaves the chair, to make a statement of the government's position on matters of external affairs in which I believe hon. members are immediately interested, and we might proceed then with the debate in a formal manner. When the debate has continued for such time as hon. members may deem sufficient, the house could then go into committee and proceed to further discussion by question and answer. I think that procedure would probably prove to be in the interest of all, but my right hon. friend the leader of the opposition may have a different view about it. If so, I should be glad before putting the motion to hear what he has to say.
Right Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Leader of the
Opposition): I am bound to say that I do entertain a different view. A motion to go into supply is not made to-morrow, and to suspend that rule for one particular purpose would be wholly improper, in my judgment, and certainly could be done only with the unanimous consent of the house. No notice being given of any such intention, inasmuch as it is an estimate for Geneva that is under consideration, the proper place for its consideration is in committee of supply when the chairman of committees is in the chair. I am sorry I do not see it as the right hon. gentleman has mentioned, but I conceive the proper manner to deal with it is the manner I have indicated, and not in the manner he has suggested.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Of course that settles the matter.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: It is a difference of opinion; that is all.

It requires unanimous consent. I had thought that by following the course I have suggested our discussion, having regard to the importance of the matters likely to be discussed, might be carried on in a more dignified and befitting manner than would otherwise be possible. However, I shall carry out the undertaking given, namely that to-morrow we would proceed in committee of supply with the consideration of the item concerning Geneva, at which time matters relating to external affairs may be discussed.
The government will be prepared to consider morning sittings any time hon. members may feel they would care to have them begin. But in this I do not wish to suggest a course which would not be wholly acceptable to my right hon. friend the leader of the opposition or to any other hon. members of the house.
